new_page.title: Living in Princeton, BC: Homes, Flood History & Schools
new_page.description: Princeton, BC for home buyers: where the Tulameen meets the Similkameen, the 2021 flood, schools, hospital, zoning, and town versus rural lots.

faq.q: How far is Princeton from the Fraser Valley?
faq.a: Princeton is 133 km east of Hope on Highway 3 (the Crowsnest Highway), and 90 km south of Merritt on Highway 5A.

faq.q: Can I add a suite to a house in Princeton?
faq.a: Under BC’s 2023 small-scale multi-unit housing law, every municipality must allow a secondary suite or a detached accessory dwelling on most single-family lots. Confirm the lot’s zone with the Town of Princeton, or with the Regional District for rural Area H.

Princeton is a town of 2,894 people (2021 census, up 2.3% from 2016) in the Similkameen Valley, where the Tulameen River runs into the Similkameen at 650 metres above sea level. It sits at the junction of Highways 3 and 5A: Hope is 133 km west on Highway 3, Merritt 90 km north on 5A and Keremeos 67 km east. Founded in 1858, it became a village in 1951 and a town in 1978. Forestry and mining built it; the Copper Mountain mine south of town is now owned by Hudbay Minerals.

items.t: Inside the town
(about 59 km²): the Town of Princeton sets zoning and runs water and sewer. Its Official Community Plan Bylaw No. 1044, 2023 was adopted December 20, 2023 and plans to 2042.
Outside the town:

rural Princeton is Electoral Area H of the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen. Its Zoning Bylaw No. 3065, 2024 (adopted July 25, 2024) replaced Bylaw No. 2498 to allow more small-scale housing; the OCP is Bylaw No. 2497, 2012. Rural homes are usually on a well and septic.
Suites:

under the Province’s 2023 small-scale multi-unit housing law, every BC municipality must allow a secondary suite or a detached accessory dwelling on most single-family lots. The three-to-four-unit rule applies only in municipalities of more than 5,000 people, and Princeton has under 3,000.
The 2021 flood:

in November 2021 the Tulameen and Similkameen rivers overflowed their banks and dikes. The Town declared a state of emergency and 290 households (571 residents) were displaced at first. The Province’s summary lists $11.9 million in interim flood support, more than $4 million of it for drinking water repairs, and funding for a flood hazard assessment of both rivers. The Town’s 2024 request for federal flood-mitigation funding was turned down.
Before you buy near either river:
ask the Town or the Regional District whether the lot is in a floodplain, check the flood history in the disclosure, and get a quote for flood coverage from your insurer before you remove conditions.

blocks.text: Schools, health care and getting around

items.t: Schools:
School District 58 (Nicola-Similkameen) runs John Allison Elementary (K–3), Vermilion Forks Elementary (4–7) and Princeton Secondary (8–12).
Health care:
Princeton General Hospital has a 6-bed acute care unit and Ridgewood Lodge, a 36-bed extended care unit.
Getting around:
Princeton Aerodrome has no scheduled flights; the nearest scheduled service is Penticton Regional Airport, with Kelowna International beyond it.
Outdoors:

the Kettle Valley Rail Trail and China Ridge trails for biking, hiking and cross-country skiing, Manning Park to the west, and fishing on both rivers. The town has a pool, a 700-seat arena, a curling rink and 14 parks.
